title: A chassis for the rover, and why it drifts
summary: Print a chassis sized to the motors and battery, wire everything up, and measure how far a commanded straight line actually drifts.
materials: the two motors, H-bridge, wheels, ESP32 and battery from week 1
masking tape for a straight reference line

figure.alt: A dashed rectangle outlines the chassis footprint from above, with a motor circle at each side and the battery box in the middle. Dimension lines mark the motor diameter and the battery's length and height, the measurements taken with calipers the day before printing and used to size the chassis in Tinkercad.

items.s: Chassis sized to motors and battery
Measured with calipers the day before printing

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The bench components from week 1 become a real chassis: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: the motors and battery worked fine sitting on a bench. Will a chassis built around them actually drive in a straight line?

Imagine: a printed chassis sized to the exact motors and battery you measured, holding everything rigid so nothing shifts while it drives.

Plan: the day before this session, measure each motor's body diameter and mounting tabs, and the battery's length, width and height, all in millimetres. Model the chassis in Tinkercad to those measurements and print it, so it is cooled and ready when this session starts.

figure.alt: Two motor boxes both commanded to 60 percent power: motor L turns at about 200 revolutions per minute, motor R at about 190. A dashed line below shows the rover drifting off a straight line as a result, illustrating how even a small speed gap between matched motors steers the rover away from straight.

items.s: A small speed gap steers the rover off straight

steps.title: Matched motors still differ
steps.body:
Two motors from the same batch are never perfectly identical. Tiny differences in friction, magnet strength and how the coil was wound survive even careful manufacturing.

Command both motors the exact same power and they still turn at slightly different speeds. Commanding the same 60 percent power, one wheel might turn at 200 revolutions a minute and the other at 190, a small but real gap.

That gap adds up. A five percent speed difference does not sound like much. Over a couple of metres of driving, it steers the rover steadily off a straight line.

Nothing is broken. This is simply what real motors do, and it is why an equal-power command is not the same thing as a straight line.

figure.alt: The rover sits at the start of a two-metre reference line taped on the floor. A dashed arrow shows its actual path curving away from the straight line, with a dimension line marking the drift distance from the reference line at the two-metre mark, in centimetres. A caption notes three commanded power levels, 40, 60 and 80 percent, were each tested three times.

items.s: Drive the 2 m line, measure drift from centre
Tested at 40%, 60% and 80% commanded power, 3 runs each

steps.title: Drive a straight line and measure the drift
steps.body:
Mount the motors, wheels, H-bridge, ESP32 and battery in the printed chassis. Wire each connection the same way it was tested on the bench in week 1.

Tape a straight reference line on the floor, at least two metres long. Set the rover on the line facing forward, and command equal power to both wheels.

Test three equal-power levels: about 40 percent, 60 percent and 80 percent. For each level, drive the full two metres. Then measure how far the rover's centre sits from the reference line, in centimetres.

Run each power level three times, nine runs in total, keeping the starting position and the reference line exactly the same every time.
checklist: The chassis holds the motors, wheels, H-bridge, ESP32 and battery, wired the same way as week 1
The reference line was at least two metres long and stayed in the same place for every run
Three equal-power levels were each tested three times, nine runs in total
The drift from the reference line was measured the same way, in centimetres, every time

steps.title: Commanded power versus drift
steps.body:
The chassis, the wiring and the reference line stay the same for every row. Only the commanded power level changes.

Test three power levels, three times each, nine rows in total. For each run, write the commanded power and the drift from the reference line in centimetres.
steps.question: Did drift get bigger or smaller at higher power, and by about how many centimetres?

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line for each thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. Classics this week: a wheel pressed on loosely, slipping on the shaft and throwing off the drift on one side only.

Also watch for a reference line that was not actually straight. And watch for a starting position that shifted slightly between runs, which makes the drift numbers impossible to trust.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the printed chassis wired up sitting on the reference line, plus your nine-row table of commanded power and measured drift
